headline: A report of an SEC accounting probe sinks Nvidia 14% and XLK 7.4%; the S&P 500 enters a correction and staples are the only sector to rise
summary: SPY fell 3.8% on Friday against 2.1% for the equal-weight RSP, a seventh straight loss that put the S&P 500 in a correction; over the past month SPY is down 9.9% and RSP 5.1%. Staples were the only sector to rise (+0.6%), with health care (−0.3%), energy (−0.8%) and utilities (−0.8%) close behind, while tech (−7.4%), industrials (−3.3%) and discretionary (−3.1%) fell most. Over the month staples (+0.4%), real estate (−0.2%) and utilities (−0.5%) hold up best, and tech (−18.4%), energy (−10.6%) and communication services (−7.0%) lag. The driver was a chip rout (SOX −10.7%) after Reuters reported SEC staff are examining Nvidia's accounting, which pushed money into Treasuries: the 10-year fell 14bp to 4.91% and the VIX jumped 26% to 35.89.
drivers: Nvidia probe report turns the chip slide into a rout

Nvidia was already down 6–7% when Reuters reported the SEC is looking at possible accounting issues; it closed −14.0% at $125.53, its worst day since January 2025. AMD, Micron and Broadcom each fell more than 12%, Broadcom on an unconfirmed report that Google will cut next year's custom-chip orders, and XLK lost 7.4%, its RSI now 28 and the price 19.3% below its 50-day.
AI losses spread to software, cyclicals and Anthropic

Intuit dropped more than 10% after cutting its fiscal 2027 revenue outlook, and Anthropic fell 8.5% to $88.91, close to its $83 IPO price. Industrials (−3.3%), discretionary (−3.1%) and communication services (−2.8%) followed tech lower; over the week SPY lost 8.7% and RSP 6.3%.
Defensives hold up as bonds rally

The 10-year fell 14bp to 4.91% and the 2-year 17bp to 4.61%, trimming December hike odds. Staples rose 0.6% and health care slipped only 0.3% as TD Cowen upgraded UnitedHealth and Humana to buy, but rate-sensitive utilities (−0.8%) and real estate (−1.0%) still fell in the broad selling.
WTI rose 0.9% to $83.98, so XLE fell only 0.8%; it is still −13.7% month to date with RSI 25 and 6.6% below its 50-day.
rotation: Communication services moved from Improving into Leading since the last recap, the only quadrant change; its 3-month relative strength is still −1.2 points, so the move reflects the cap-weighted index falling faster rather than strength of its own. That leaves eight sectors in Leading (staples, health care, utilities, financials, real estate, discretionary, industrials and communication services), energy and materials in Weakening and tech alone in Lagging. Staples (+13.6 points), health care (+11.3) and utilities (+9.0) remain the strongest, energy's relative strength rose to +5.9 points as it fell less than SPY, and materials crept back to +0.1. Tech is at −7.7 points and 19.3% below its 50-day, the widest gap on the page. The defensive rotation ends when XLK reclaims its 50-day average with creations continuing and staples and health care start losing relative strength; Friday pushed that further out.
flows: State Street flows to Nov 19 show ETF holders still buying tech into the slide: XLK took in $300m in a week, $2.66bn in a month (2.5% of assets) and $3.93bn over 3 months, while its price fell 18.4% in a month. The selling has spread to the sectors that held up: health care lost $912m in a week (1.9% of assets) and energy $1.14bn (3.0%), taking energy's monthly outflow to $1.72bn (4.4%). Utilities lost $1.67bn in a month (7.2% of assets) and staples $379m (2.6%) even as they led on price, so the defensive bid looks institutional rather than ETF-driven. Financials keep bleeding ($713m in a week, $3.19bn over 3 months), while materials took in $351m in a month (4.4% of assets, the most on the page). For scale, SPY lost $6.96bn in the week (0.9% of its $0.76tn) and $3.30bn over the month, so broad beta is now being sold while sector ETF buyers keep averaging into tech.
model: The six-factor model, now using FactSet's Nov 20 valuations, still ranks energy first (77), then health care (62), staples (58), materials (55), financials (50) and real estate (50, up from seventh after gaining a valuation input). Tech slipped to seventh (48) from fifth as its 3-month relative strength fell to −7.7 points, utilities (41) moved past discretionary (41) into eighth, and industrials (37) and communication services (32) stay at the bottom. Energy's lead rests on +55% 12-1 month momentum, an 11.5x forward P/E and 151% Q3 earnings growth, while its 1-month outflows (4.4% of assets) and RSI 25 point the other way, so I stay neutral. Utilities are held back by the worst flow score (−7.2% of assets). I am more constructive than the model on tech, where 73% Q3 earnings growth, a 16.7x forward P/E and continuing inflows offset the trend, but I am not adding while the Nvidia probe is unresolved.
weightsSrc: Schwab Center for Financial Research, as of Oct 2, 2026; rolled forward by each sector ETF's price change

XLV.view: Health care slipped only 0.3% as TD Cowen upgraded UnitedHealth and Humana to buy and named UnitedHealth its best idea for 2027, which eased some of the pressure from the Medicare Advantage audit proposal. XLV is −2.4% over a month against −9.9% for SPY, and fund managers raised their health care overweight in BofA's November survey. At 19.7x forward earnings it is cheaper than staples, which is why I keep the overweight.
XLV.modelView: Second (62, down from 64): +11.3 points of 3-month relative strength and the strongest trend (10.6% above the 200-day). Weak spots are 9% Q3 earnings growth, RSI 37 and $912m of redemptions in the latest week (1.9% of assets).
XLV.trade: Hold the overweight through pharma, tools and now the large managed-care names; cut to neutral on a close below the 50-day average (the price is just 0.3% above it).
XLV.risk: The audit rule spreading to a wider Medicare Advantage squeeze; crowded defensive positioning unwinding if tech rebounds sharply.

XLF.view: Financials fell 2.0% and are 2.5% below the 50-day average, so the neutral stance set on Thursday holds. The bond rally (10-year −14bp to 4.91%) trims the margin tailwind, and ETF redemptions continue ($713m in a week). At 14.4x forward earnings (FactSet) the sector is the second cheapest after energy.
XLF.modelView: Fifth (50, from sixth): +3.5 points of 3-month relative strength and 1.4% above the 200-day, held back by flows ($886m out in a month, 1.7% of assets) and modest 12-1 month momentum (+12%).
XLF.trade: Neutral; move back to overweight on a close above the 50-day average with weekly redemptions stopping, and prefer large money-centre banks and brokers over regionals.
XLF.risk: Private-credit or commercial real estate losses; trading and deal activity slowing if the correction deepens.

XLK.view: Tech fell 7.4% as Nvidia dropped 14% on the report of an SEC accounting review and chip names fell more than 12%, while Intuit's outlook cut dragged on software. XLK is −18.4% over a month and RSI 28, yet Q3 earnings grew 73% (FactSet) and the sector trades at about 16.7x forward earnings, below the market. The probe adds a governance risk to the biggest AI holding that valuation alone cannot price, so I keep the stance but pause new buying.
XLK.modelView: Seventh (48, down from fifth): the worst 3-month relative strength (−7.7 points) and a price 13.0% below the 200-day now outweigh +30% 12-1 month momentum, strong valuation and earnings scores and 1-month inflows of 2.5% of assets.
XLK.trade: Neutral with one tranche in; add the second only after a close back above the 50-day average (19.3% above) or clarity on the Nvidia review, whichever comes first.
XLK.risk: Confirmation of accounting problems at Nvidia, or a hyperscaler capex cut, which 52% of BofA's surveyed managers expect within six months.

XLP.view: Staples were the only sector to rise on Friday (+0.6%) and lead the month (+0.4%), with Walmart extending gains after its raised outlook. At 23.3x forward earnings (FactSet) the sector costs about 36% more than the market, and ETF holders are still selling ($379m out in a month).
XLP.modelView: Third (58, up from 54): the strongest 3-month relative strength (+13.6 points) and 7.3% above the 200-day, with a weak valuation score and outflows of 2.6% of assets in a month.
XLP.trade: Neutral; keep trimming into haven rallies and rotate into pharma within health care.
XLP.risk: A deeper growth scare would extend the defensive bid.

XLE.view: Energy fell 0.8% as WTI rose 0.9% to $83.98. It is the cheapest sector (11.5x forward earnings) with the fastest Q3 earnings growth (151%, FactSet), but XLE is −13.7% month to date, RSI 25, and ETF holders pulled $1.14bn in a week. Crude still has not regained the mid-$80s.
XLE.modelView: First in the model (77): valuation, earnings and 12-1 month momentum (+55%) carry it, while price (−10.6% in a month), flows (−4.4% of assets in a month) and the Weakening quadrant point the other way, which is why I don't follow the model's overweight.
XLE.trade: Neutral; don't add until WTI regains $85 and XLE recloses above its 50-day average (now 6.6% below it); oversold readings alone are not a signal.
XLE.risk: Further surplus-driven oil weakness; Gulf escalation is the upside risk.

XLB.view: Materials fell 2.3% with the cyclicals and are −8.5% month to date, 5.2% below the 200-day with RSI 24. Q3 earnings grew about 30% (FactSet) and the sector trades at about 16.9x forward earnings, and ETF buyers keep adding ($351m in a month).
XLB.modelView: Fourth (55): 1-month inflows of 4.4% of assets, the best flow score on the page, and +23% 12-1 month momentum, against flat 3-month relative strength (+0.1 points) and a price 5.2% below the 200-day.
XLB.trade: Neutral; wait for a close back above the 200-day before adding, and prefer data-center materials over miners.
XLB.risk: A stronger dollar and slower China demand.

XLC.view: Communication services fell 2.8% as AI-linked names slid with Anthropic; XLC is −7.0% over a month and −14.4% this year. Q3 earnings grew about 18% (FactSet) and the sector trades at about 16.2x forward earnings, the cheapest after energy and financials, and ETF buyers added $196m in the latest week.
XLC.modelView: Last (32): flat 12-1 month momentum (−2%), 10.4% below the 200-day and $565m of outflows in a month (2.7% of assets). It moved into Leading on the rotation map only because SPY fell faster.
XLC.trade: Neutral; a bounce candidate if tech turns, but it needs to reclaim its 200-day average first.
XLC.risk: More AI capex without matching revenue; advertising slowing if the consumer weakens.

XLI.view: Industrials fell 3.3%, the second-worst sector, and are −12.6% over three months as the AI-power equipment trade keeps unwinding. At 21.3x forward earnings (FactSet) they still trade at a premium to the market. Morgan Stanley picks the sector for 2027.
XLI.modelView: Tenth (37): −3.0 points of 3-month relative strength, 9.6% below the 200-day, RSI 30 and a poor valuation score. Flows are small: $48m in over a month, $114m out in the latest week.
XLI.trade: Underweight; keep aerospace and defence, and revisit electrical equipment only on a close back above the 200-day.
XLI.risk: A fast AI-capex rebound would lift the electrical-equipment names first.

XLY.view: Discretionary fell 3.1%, the third-worst sector, as the selling spread from tech into cyclicals; XLY is −5.4% this year. At 24.2x forward earnings (FactSet) it is the most expensive sector, and the holiday season now decides the call.
XLY.modelView: Ninth (41, down from eighth): +4.7 points of 3-month relative strength but 2.4% below the 200-day, weak 12-1 month momentum (+3%) and the weakest valuation score; $112m of creations in a month.
XLY.trade: Underweight; move to neutral only if Black Friday and Cyber Monday data confirm spending and XLY regains its 200-day average.
XLY.risk: A strong holiday season or an Amazon-led re-rating forcing the move to neutral sooner.

XLU.view: Utilities fell 0.8% despite the 14bp drop in the 10-year, and ETF holders keep selling ($148m in a week, $1.67bn in a month). At about 16.8x forward earnings they are no longer expensive, and Morgan Stanley is overweight on power demand, but the AI-power link cuts both ways in this selloff.
XLU.modelView: Eighth (41, up from ninth after gaining a valuation input): +9.0 points of 3-month relative strength, but flat 12-1 month momentum and the worst flow score (−7.2% of assets in a month); RSI 37 and 2.9% below the 200-day.
XLU.trade: Underweight; use haven bounces to reduce, and revisit if monthly redemptions stop with the 10-year below 5%.
XLU.risk: A sustained bond rally or a sharper risk-off move.

XLRE.view: Real estate fell 1.0% even as the 10-year dropped to 4.91%, and is −0.2% over the month. At about 17.7x forward earnings it trades just above the market, and office and retail still face refinancing at much higher rates.
XLRE.modelView: Sixth (50, up from seventh after gaining a valuation input): +4.0 points of relative strength, a positive 20-day money flow (CMF +0.05) and $45m of creations in a month, against weak 12-1 month momentum (+9%) and a price 1.4% below the 200-day.
XLRE.trade: Underweight the sector; prefer data-center and health-care REITs if exposure is needed, and move to neutral if the 10-year holds below 4.9% and XLRE regains its 200-day.
XLRE.risk: A further fall in long yields would spark a sharp short-covering rally.
